channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: Jeep Madness In Borneo
item.description: Among the last RAAF officers to leave Borneo, Keith Dunstan rides the North Borneo jungle railway behind a jeep fitted with railway bogies, a five-hour pushing, sliding, landslide-crashing journey to Beaufort and on to Tenom.

item.title: Where A Fellow Finds A Friend
item.description: A visit to the new Victoria Police boys' club behind Fitzroy Town Hall, where constables, Fitzroy footballers and Ben Barnett coach inner-suburban lads who would otherwise be roaming the streets.

item.title: Life Begins at Seven-Ten
item.description: A comic account of the silent, clubbish regulars on the early bus to work, followed by a train journey to Melbourne spent with a port-swigging airman, swinging kitbags and three mischievous schoolgirls.

item.title: Obsession
item.description: A short story, published in The Herald's short story series, about a jam-factory hand terrified of snakes since childhood who survives the Middle East campaign only to face his real fear in a jungle in the islands.

item.title: There's Glitter In New Hongkong
item.description: Fresh from a year in the Pacific, Keith Dunstan finds post-war Hong Kong one big black market of pre-war luxuries, glittering multinational cabarets and stripped, firewood-looted flats, overshadowed by a Japanese war memorial on the island's highest peak.

item.title: Taking the Doomba out of Moomba
item.description: Melbourne Tourism Authority director Sue Calwell fights to change Melburnians' self-deprecating habit of knocking their own city — a habit so ingrained that Barry Humphries' proposal to turn City Square into an abyss called "Doomba" received more press than any promotional campaign.

item.title: Cashing in on nostalgia
item.description: The Victorian Government's $100,000 competition for a "Melbourne Monument" to rival the Eiffel Tower prompts Dunstan's winning entry — rebuilding Old Melbourne complete with Cole's Book Arcade, cable trams, the Port Phillip Hotel's punkahs, and all the great Victorian drapery stores with their real counters and real service, a nostalgia trap that would draw tourists by the million.

item.title: Knockers held in high regard
item.description: Lord Mayor Rockman's campaign against Melbourne knockers — with his proposed "I love Melbourne" bumper stickers and appeals for positive slogans — misunderstands the fundamental psychology of Melburnians, who are kygmies by nature and would draw far more tourists with an international knocking competition than with any amount of civic boosterism.

item.title: For sale: Australia's most magnificent folly
item.description: Idylwilde, the Balwyn mansion built by chain-store magnate Oliver Gilpin in the 1930s — 230,000 pounds of Japanese gardens, canals, seven stone bridges, 35 aviaries with running water, a deer sanctuary, a hidden indoor swimming pool, and a bathroom the nuns never entered — goes to auction after the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart can no longer afford the $15,000 annual rates.

item.title: Dame Edna bares all — in limp and stiff
item.description: Dame Edna Everage arrives by Rolls-Royce with a mounted police escort and the Dandenong Marching Grannies to launch her Coffee Table Book — a guide to gracious living featuring funnel web spider cake, Norm's prostate diagram, and poems denouncing Melbourne's massage parlors.

item.title: A far cry — or yodel — from Bazza
item.description: On the set of Bruce Beresford's "The Getting of Wisdom," Barry Humphries plays a pious Presbyterian headmaster while a young Susannah Fowle takes the lead role of Laura — a world away from Bazza McKenzie, with the original PLC demolished and scenes shot at Illawarra's grand staircase.

item.title: Recalling a great Australian eccentric
item.description: A Melbourne University Gallery exhibition marks Percy Grainger's birthday and directs visitors to the remarkable Grainger Museum at the university — a repository Grainger designed and partly built himself, containing his towelling suits, his mother's clothes, freeform music machines, intimate confessions, and 21 PhDs worth of yet-unexplored material.

item.title: My secret dossier
item.description: "Batman" confesses his ASIO dossier to prove that history shows Australia's real enemies have always come from the right, not the left, by listing his own impeccably conservative credentials including Melbourne Grammar, the Melbourne Club, and devotion to Henry Bolte candles.

item.title: A serious case of maladjustment
item.description: Dunstan offers himself as an image consultant to Prime Minister Malcolm Fraser, prescribing contact lenses, a moustache, gay shirts, a cook book, C. J. Dennis poetry readings at Moomba, and a daily bicycle ride to Parliament House.

item.title: Pro Hart: a painter as busy as a bull ant
item.description: Dunstan profiles Pro Hart — the Broken Hill mining artist whom critics spurn and the public adores — tracing his childhood correspondence schooling, 15 years underground, the discovery by Kym Bonython, and his current plans for a 15-metre steel bull ant and a salt-pan canvas dropped from a balloon.

item.title: The sport of king-hits
item.description: Victoria's thumping 100-point State of Origin victory over Western Australia — achieved after Ron Barassi made his players write 300-word essays on why they wanted to play for Victoria — does nothing to ease the growing tension between States, and the VFL's rivalry with the nascent national football competition remains unresolved.

item.title: Lunch hour in a tippler's Valhalla
item.description: Melbourne's Expovin wine exhibition drew 100,000 enthusiasts to its 4½-acre floor of stands serving fine reds, pates and champagne — where Malcolm Fraser sampled only Australian wines, Wolf Blass was first in the queue, the Connoisseurs' Terrace poured 1955 Grange Hermitage, and a battery-powered home-bottling pump replaced the age-old pleasure of sucking on a tube.

item.title: Feeling the strain of the party frenzy
item.description: Keith Dunstan surveys the exhausting social demands of the Christmas party season, from the strain of remembering names after the divorce revolution to a handy list of conversation-starter topics for the desperate guest.

item.title: What did YOU do for private enterprise, daddy?
item.description: Bob Ansett's relentless battle to break the airport car-hire monopoly held by his father Sir Reginald Ansett's Avis franchise, told through his series of increasingly elaborate PR stunts.

item.title: How to keep Norm in his place
item.description: A visit to a friend's new video games set for a "sports evening" reveals the humiliating truth that the future will demand joysticks, speed-up switches, and total defeat at electronic tennis, squash, and shooting games.

item.title: Getting in the swim, and out of it
item.description: The reality of South Yarra swimming pool ownership — an hour's labour a day vacuuming leaves, wrestling with pH levels, replacing pumps at $200 a time, and suffering exploding underwater lights — proves more exhausting than a hectare of lawn.

item.title: Something to be done? Get Lillian
item.description: A portrait of Lillian Frank, Melbourne's flamboyant queen of hairdressing, whose 15-year reign of spectacular fashion at the Cup, seven front pages at Hair's opening night, and newly acquired role promoting Rocky Mattioli's world title fight proves she is as far from shy as Eva Gabor.

item.title: I'm sorry, Jim, I can't bare it
item.description: Writing from South Yarra as "Batman," Keith Dunstan explains to Jim Cairns in an open letter why his puritan Melbourne upbringing, school-day segregation, and traumatic experience at Hiroshima airport have left him constitutionally unable to participate in nude protests.

item.title: Fast becoming the land of milk and money
item.description: The Victorian Dairy Industry Authority's Big M campaign — four flavoured milk flavours in handy cartons aimed at teenagers — has captured 13 percent of the soft drink market in four weeks, and now they want to put milk cocktails into hotel smorgasbords, served as a Misky or a Cooper Special.

item.title: A burning passion for pies
item.description: Two visiting food experts — American diet guru Lelord Kordel who condemns pies, and British food scientist Dr Magnus Pyke who enthusiastically endorses them — give Dunstan the perfect excuse to confess a lifelong addiction to junk food, from penny Nestlé bars through liquorice fishing lines to the greatest Melbourne contribution to mankind, the Little Bourke Street dim sim.

item.title: The language takes a mauling
item.description: The opening of the first block of the Bourke Street Mall — complete with orange trams still running through it — prompts a meditation on the word "mall," the years of furious political warfare between Bourke Street and Collins Street factions, and the dream of one day turning Melbourne's entire Golden Mile into a pedestrian paradise.

item.title: The drama of beer-bottled wine
item.description: After attending a Brown Brothers Home Bottling Seminar where the winemakers proved a 1962 red sealed with a crown cap beat the same wine under cork, Dunstan overcomes his cultural inhibitions and finally makes the switch — bottling his cabernet-malbec in beer bottles, then wondering if the BYO restaurants will still treat him with charm.

item.title: When a mystery put Melbourne on the map
item.description: The Sun Books reprint of Fergus Hume's 1886 novel The Mystery of a Hansom Cab — which sold nearly a million copies and did more for Melbourne's fame than Nellie Melba — reveals a vanished gas-lit city of Marvellous Melbourne, the Block, Bourke Street's demi-monde, and a murder mystery that kept Batman reading until 3.30 am.

item.title: A strange path to rectitude
item.description: The 1978 Craft Festival opens with Premier Hamer and Eric Westbrook in YOU CAN MAKE IT T-shirts, 10,000 ceramic bricks to decorate, and a stained glass panel for the front door that the wife quietly had a professional redo — leaving Dunstan to wonder if by December the whole city will be praying for the return of Norm.

item.title: From now on, Horrie suits himself
item.description: Horrie Taafe, the unquestionable men's wear fashion czar of Australia who revolutionised Georges and took buying tours to Harrods in the 1930s, is retiring for the third time — to open his own shop at Mona Vale at nearly 80, with his lifelong hatreds of denim, flared trousers and body-hugging shirts intact.
